\section{Label and Exit}
\seclabel{label-expr}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{DelimitedExpr} &::=&
\KWD{label} \emph{Id} \emph{BlockElems} \KWD{end} \emph{Id} \\

\emph{FlowExpr}
&::=& \KWD{exit} \option{\emph{Id}} \options{\KWD{with} \emph{Expr}} \\

\end{Grammar}

An expression block may be labeled using a \KWD{label} expression,
which consists of \KWD{label}, an identifier (the block's \emph{name}),
an expression block (its \emph{body}), \KWD{end}, and finally its name again
(it is a static error if the identifier after \KWD{end} is not the name).
The name of a \KWD{label} expression
is in scope in the label namespace
at any point in its body
that is not within a \KWD{spawn} subexpression of the body.
A \KWD{label} expression is evaluated
by evaluating its body.

An \KWD{exit} expression consists of \KWD{exit},
an optional identifier (the \emph{target})
and an optional \KWD{with} clause,
which consists of \KWD{with} followed by an expression.
If a target is specified, it is
a static error if the target is not in scope
in the label namespace at the \KWD{exit} expression.
That is, the target must be the name
of a statically enclosing \KWD{label} expression,
and the \KWD{exit} expression must not be within
a \KWD{spawn} expression that is contained
in the \KWD{label} expression.
If no target is specified, the target is implicitly the name
of the smallest statically enclosing \KWD{label} expression; it is
a static error if there is no such expression.

An \KWD{exit} expression with a \KWD{with} clause
evaluates its \KWD{with} clause expression to yield a \KWD{with} clause value.
The \KWD{exit} expression completes abruptly with the \KWD{with} clause value
(see \secref{eval-completion}).
An \KWD{exit} expression with no \KWD{with} clause
has an implicit \KWD{with} clause whose expression is \EXP{()}.
The type of an \KWD{exit} expression is \TYP{BottomType}.

If the evaluation of the body of a \KWD{label} expression completes normally,
its value is the value of the body.
If the evaluation of the body completes abruptly
with an \KWD{exit} expression whose target
is the name of the \KWD{label} expression,
then the evaluation of the \KWD{label} expression completes normally
and its value is the \KWD{with} clause value of the \KWD{exit} expression.
The type of a \KWD{label} expression
is the union of the type of the last expression of its expression block
and the types of the \KWD{with} clause values of
any \KWD{exit} expressions within the \KWD{label} expression
whose target is the \KWD{label} expression's name.

If one or more \KWD{try} expressions are nested between an
\KWD{exit} expression and the targeted \KWD{label} block, the \KWD{finally}
clauses of these expressions are run in order, from innermost to
outermost, as described in \secref{try-expr}.  If any \KWD{finally}
clause completes abruptly by throwing an exception, the \KWD{exit}
expression fails to exit, the evaluation of the \KWD{label} expression
completes abruptly, and the exception is propagated.

Here is a simple example:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.Label.tex}
The expression ``\EXP{\KWD{exit} I_{95} \KWD{with} \VAR{x32B}}'' completes
abruptly and attempts to transfer control to the end of the
targeted labeled block ``\EXP{\KWD{label} I_{95}}''.
The targeted labeled block completes normally with value \VAR{x32B}.

## In short

- **The question.** `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]` and `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]` add, subtract and multiply values of `T` in their bodies, and the scalar-extension block adds, subtracts, `MIN`s and `MAX`es a `T` with each element of an `Array[\T,I\]`; `Number` declares `asFloat` and `=` and nothing else. Which bound on `T` gives those bodies their arithmetic? It holds 25 of the 153 errors the compiled checker reports on the one library: 15 arithmetic refusals at `(T, T)` or `T`, the 8 of the scalar block, and 2 "does not satisfy the bound" sites at the factories `vector` and `matrix` (section 1).
- **What the history says.** The team's bound did carry arithmetic. Their `Number` extended `AdditiveGroup[\Number\]`, `MultiplicativeRing[\Number\]` and `StandardMinMax[\Number\]` and declared `+`, `-`, juxtaposition and `MIN` on any two numbers, every result an `RR64` (`git show 75cca6683:Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, lines 273-313). Route A, his decision, took that arithmetic off `Number` and gave it to each sibling at its own type (POSITIONS, "The exclusion rule stays and the tower is flat (route A)"; `d846e3644`). The fork is the obligation route A left on the arrays (FACTS, "Route A's generic container obligations still need body-level checks"). The bound that says on the flat tower what the team's bound said on theirs is "a number that is a ring at its own type".
- **The library's own way.** Since answer 7 the library bounds generic arithmetic by its algebra trait at the element's type: `SUM[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\]`, `PROD[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3284-3301`), and where one trait is not enough it writes two, `MaxSumReductionPair[\T extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], StandardMax[\T\] }\]` (`:3262`, `:3268`). Its products are methods so that views override them: `TransposedMatrix` overrides `scale`, `rmul` and `lmul` (`:2800-2802`), and his diagonal overrides `mul` (POSITIONS, "The vocabulary's scalar drops and the diagonal").
- **The recommendation.** The library's two-trait bound, each declaration asking for what its body uses: `Vector`, `Matrix`, their storing objects, factories, norms and products take `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` (29 component lines, 32 api lines); the scalar block takes a bound per operator, `{ Number, AdditiveGroup[\T\] }` on `+` and `-`, `{ Number, StandardMin[\T\] }` on `MIN`, `{ Number, StandardMax[\T\] }` on `MAX` (8 and 8). `Number` stays, so its exclusions, its `asFloat` and the specification's "all elements of vectors and matrices must be numbers" stay; the algebra trait brings the arithmetic. No body, model or specification line changes. On the flat tower every number type is a ring at its own type, the integers included (`Integral[\I\] extends MultiplicativeRing[\I\]`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:443`), so no integer array is excluded. **Default: the same.**
- **Measured today** (section 3), on a copy of the library through the gate's distance stage and under walk: the type-check stage clears all 23 arithmetic and block sites and uncovers the one parent-trait error at `scale` (`:2399`), as read; the two factory sites stay, as read; walk's seven array tests print the same as on the unchanged copy. And one thing not read: the checker's overloading stage crashes on the api and the component, and the export stage with it, "ClassCastException: UnionType cannot be cast to BaseType" in the team's `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.boundsSubstitution` (`TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:474-477`, David Chase, 2012, "TODO: FIX THIS FOR OPS", unchanged since), because the checker reads the closed `Number` as the union of its members and the meet of two bounds then comes back a union. One call is refused for the same reason (the norm's `squaredNorm(me)`, `:2483`). So the way needs a checker fix first, and the 09-29 timing question is not answered: the Meet Rule check that was slow then did not run today.
- **A batch 13 rung, in two halves** (section 5): the checker's `boundsSubstitution` taught a bound list whose meet is a union, test first with an expected-failure compiled test; then the 77 library lines, the distance stage before and after by row and line. It clears 23 of the fork's 25 and uncovers 1: 153 to about 131.
- **What it leaves.** The 2 factory sites, a checker slip no bound cures (section 2.2); the bodies typed by the parent trait, 10 with `:2399`, which need their own list of ways; row 437's numeral `0` in `matrix(v)`, whose repair `v.zero` the bound now permits; a `Vector` of numerals (`IntLiteral` is a `Number` and not a ring), which nothing on record makes; walk's `Bottom` for a two-bound parameter that no call fixes (row 591), which the arrays' calls all fix; the code generator's erasure of a two-trait bound, unmeasured, which `MaxSumReductionPair` already carries to the switch-over.
- **What it bends.** The letter of "no blanket ring bound" on the two traits, not its reason (integer arrays), and the placement of the array questions after the switch-over, which PLAN's batch 13 line already brings forward for this fork (section 6).

### 2.9 The ways, judged

1. **6a, `T extends Number`, as landed.** Keeps 25 errors; the bodies have no evidence for their arithmetic. Out.
2. **6b, the storing objects take their traits' bound.** Landed by batch 12's rung S (`74b28e9d4`); 19 sites gone, none new. Done.
3. **6c alone, `T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`.** Measured 09-29 (RINGVM): all 36 of V1 went and 8 came, because the ring is open where `Number` is closed: 4 overloading errors against the library's juxtapositions with a `String`, the norm's `asFloat`, the two factory sites again, one size-losing join uncovered; on the scalar block walk refused `MAX` at load, "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types" (FACTS, "The shipped `RR64` ..."). It also makes "all elements of vectors and matrices must be numbers" false. It is the one way that does not meet the checker's crash (no closed trait in the bound), and the only way to buy that is to lose `Number`. Out.
4. **6c in the library's two-trait form, `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`, on the array family, with a bound per operator on the scalar block.** Measured 09-29 on the traits alone (RINGNUM): 34 of 36 went, 1 came (the join at today's `:2420`, already on today's list), the two factory sites stayed; walk's seven array tests printed the same; the checker took 3,825 s against 704 s in the Meet Rule's exclusion tests through the `comprises` check, code that rung O then rewrote. Measured today (section 3): the type-check stage clears the 23 and uncovers `:2399`; walk's seven tests print the same; and the overloading stage crashes in `boundsSubstitution` on the same `comprises` expansion (section 2.2), with one call refused at the norm. It keeps every exclusion, `asFloat` and the specification's sentences; it admits every number type but the numeral type. **Recommended, with the checker fix as the rung's first half.**
5. **6d, a bound per operation inside the traits.** `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` on the traits for `+` and `-`, the ring only where a product is taken. The products are methods (section 2.5); a method with a bound of its own needs a `where` clause, unsupported, the same wall as row 433's fusion pairs ("Fix: `where { T extends StandardMax[\T\] }` per overload once method `where` clauses work"). Moving the products out of the traits into top-level functions takes `TransposedMatrix`'s overrides and his diagonal's `mul` with them, against the library's own pattern and his decision of 2026-09-24. On the flat tower it would gain nothing: no number type is outside the ring. And every bound it would write beside `Number` meets the same crash. So 6d is the refinement for the day `where` clauses exist, not a way now. Its spirit is kept where it costs nothing, on the block's top-level operators. Not measured, by reading; no probe was needed to see the wall.
6. **6e, the specification's `Ring` and `Field`.** Operator parameters and `where` clauses first; the library's statement of them is commented out. Later, with the algebraic layer.
7. **6f, arithmetic on `Number`.** `opr +(self, other: Number): Number` loses `T` and reverses route A. Out.

## 4. The recommendation, the default, what it changes and costs

**Recommended: the library's two-trait bound, each declaration asking for what its body uses.**

- `Vector`, `Matrix`, `__DefaultVector`, `__DefaultMatrix`, `TransposedMatrix`, the factories `vector`, `tabulatedVector`, `matrix`, `pmul`, `squaredNorm`, the norm, and every sized `DOT` and juxtaposition of the family: `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`. 29 lines of `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` (`:2391-2871`), 32 of `.fsi` (`:1602-1785`).
- The scalar block: `+` and `-` take `T extends { Number, AdditiveGroup[\T\] }`, `MIN` takes `{ Number, StandardMin[\T\] }`, `MAX` takes `{ Number, StandardMax[\T\] }`. 8 lines of `.fss` (`:4716-4726`), 8 of `.fsi` (`:2681-2691`).

**Default**, for him to accept without reading the argument: the same. It is the library's own two forms (answer 7's algebra bound and the two-trait bound) applied to the one family that still carries the team's pre-route-A bound.

**What it changes.** 77 lines of bound text, no body, no model line (`RR64` satisfies the bound; `Diag` and every `vector[\RR64,n\]` of C4 unchanged), no specification sentence made false, no Appendix I entry (the library's bounds are the library's; the specification's three sentences on `Number` elements stay true). It opens row 437's repair: `matrix(v)`'s off-diagonal `0` can become `v.zero`, which `AdditiveGroup` gives `T` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:260`).

**What it costs.** Two halves of one batch 13 rung: a checker fix of the team's `boundsSubstitution` first, since without it the library's overloading and export stages crash and hide their errors (section 3), then the library lines. Under walk nothing. The checker's time on the library after the fix is unmeasured; the cause of the 09-29 cost is the cause of today's crash, so the fix that unexpands the closed bound should settle both (section 3). A `Vector` whose element type is the numeral type `IntLiteral` no longer satisfies the bound: nothing on record makes one (`IntLiteral` is the type of a numeral before it reaches a typed slot, FACTS, "The one library's numeral type is the compiler library's `IntLiteral` ..."), and the seven array tests and `FlatTowerRungF`'s 72 assertions over seven number types pass under walk with the bound (section 3).

**What it does not do.** It does not give `Vector` or `Matrix` elementwise `×` or `/` (rows 109, 293), does not touch the exclusion `excludes { AnyMultiplicativeRing }` (the vector is not a ring; its element is), and does not decide the width, decision D or decision A.

## For Pavol

A *bound* is the rule on a type parameter. `Vector[\T extends Number\]` says the elements are numbers. The team's `Number` carried plus, minus and times itself. Route A, your decision, moved that arithmetic to each number type at its own type, through the library's algebra traits: `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` gives plus and minus, `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]` those and times. So `Vector`'s body adds two `T`s and the checker finds no rule for it: 25 of the 153 errors.

The library already bounds generic arithmetic by the algebra trait (`SUM`, `PROD`), and writes two traits where one is not enough: `T extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], StandardMax[\T\] }`.

I recommend both:

- `Vector`, `Matrix` and their family: `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`. "Elements are numbers" stays; the ring brings the arithmetic.
- The scalar block, the array-with-number operators: a bound per operator. `+` and `-` get `AdditiveGroup`; `MIN` and `MAX` get `StandardMin` and `StandardMax`.

Every number type is a ring, integers included, so no integer array is excluded. Your check "no blanket ring bound that would exclude integer arrays" keeps its reason, not its letter.

Measured today: 23 of the 25 errors go, 1 hidden one appears, walk's seven array tests print the same. Found: the checker's overloading check (team code, 2012) crashes on a two-trait bound when one trait is closed like `Number`. So the rung has two halves: that checker fix, test first, then the 77 library lines.

No body, model or specification line changes. It leaves 2 errors (a checker slip at two factories) and 10 that need their own list of ways.

Rejected: the ring alone (loses `Number`'s exclusions); a bound per method (needs `where` clauses, unbuilt, and breaks your diagonal's override); arithmetic on `Number` (reverses route A).

Recommendation: the two-trait bound, one batch 13 rung in two halves. Default: the same.

## How a defect is recorded

Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:

1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. If walk crashes on the program, still write the `XXX` test, unlike under 3: the harness counts the crash as the expected failure. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, or no gated test can pass while it shows, as when walk crashes on the program, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.

If your brief does not let you edit the original tree, say in your report which of the three the defect needs, and write a ledger row for it, whichever it needs. The change that next works there writes the test.

## The order: the test, its failure, the fix, the pass

1. Write the test, with a plain name. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
2. Run the test's program through the harness before you run it any other way. In that Bash call, echo a line that starts `Expected failure:` before the harness command. In that line, say how the harness should report the failure. Then see the test fail that way through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build or compile your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. If your tree already holds the fix, run the test through the harness on the old code, as `worktrees.md`, "Running the old code", says. If the test passes, or fails another way, find out why and correct it before you make the fix. Then echo the expected failure again in the Bash call that runs the test again. If the run meets a second defect, record it as "How a defect is recorded" says.
3. Make the fix. See the test pass in your last run after your last change of code.

The test needs no commit of its own. A test that comes with no fix has no failing run: see it pass through the harness.

In your report, quote each `Expected failure:` line as the call echoed it, two to five lines of each failing run, and the passing line, each run with its command. Give the cause of each run that failed another way. In an edit of the original tree, put every check into a gated test, never into a one-off script. A task that only measures may use its own script. Assert a value with `assert` in an interpreter test. In a compiled test, assert it with `assert` (above), or print it and check it with a `run_out_equals` key.

An edit of prose in `Specification/` or `Documentation/` has no test. Check it as `specification.md`, "Changing the text: the revision form", says.

## Writing an `XXX` test

In a compiled test folder, name the component `XXXName`, in its file `XXXName.fss` and in its `component` line.

- For a refusal at compile time, write one `XXX` compile test, with `compile` and `compile_err_contains=<the refusal's message>`.
- For a code-generator wall (`compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet"), write `XXXName.test` with `tests=XXXName`, `compile` and `compile_exception_contains=<text of the exception>`.
- For a program that compiles and fails at run time, write two `.test` files over the component:

**Answer to the curator.** The rung cannot be cut as you word it, for three reasons.

A method that reads `self.n` cannot know at compile time whether some caller up the stack is inside `atomic`. The per-access `BaseTask.inATransaction()` check is how the code finds out. A plain JVM field with no check would reopen row 319, a var field outside the transaction, which the cell repaired. `compiler_tests/AtomicFieldCompiled` would fail. ## 3. A rung on the transaction check of `var` fields

**Answer to the curator.** The rung cannot be cut as you word it, for three reasons.

1. "Outside `atomic`" is a run-time fact, not a place in the source. The specification makes every read and write "which occur as part of this evaluation" of an atomic body atomic, against any action "dynamically outside" (`Specification/basic/expressions/atomic.tex:38-41`). A method that reads `self.n` cannot know at compile time whether some caller up the stack is inside `atomic`. The per-access `BaseTask.inATransaction()` check is how the code finds out. A plain JVM field with no check would reopen row 319, a var field outside the transaction, which the cell repaired. `compiler_tests/AtomicFieldCompiled` would fail. A plain field captured by a loop body or a closure would also bring back the copied-field bug that `VarFieldCapturedCompiled` gates (rung-atomic-expr-field REPORT, "Defects", item 3).
2. The walk half has no ground. Row 641 is compiled-path only: under walk its probe did not even load. Walk's tasks and transactions are a separate implementation (F-179), and the record holds no measurement of a walk var field's cost. Keeping the two paths alike is no reason to change walk's code without a measured cost and its own test.
3. The representation is still open in the record. F-374: "The batch's planner chose the cell as a default, and the curator has not decided it."

There is also a matter of payoff. microGPT has no object `var` fields. Its mutable state is three locals, `p`, `m` and `v` (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:83-89`). Row 641's measured cost is on locals: 64 % of the array loop, 9 to 15 % of the scalar loop. Its "Not measured" list names a `var` field.

**What you must decide first.** Whether the cell stays as the representation of a `var` field (F-374's default). Second, whether an `atomic` block must keep covering accesses made in code it calls, which `atomic.tex` says it must, so that any cheaper scheme still gives that guarantee.

**A rung that can be cut now.** A measurement rung, possibly followed by a check that costs less but means the same. Key lines of its brief:
- May change: `runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java`'s `inATransaction` path and `compiler/codegen/VarCodeGen.java` (`MutableStaticBinding`, `MutableFieldVar`, `LocalMutableVar`, `MutableTaskVarCodeGen`), and new tests under `compiler_tests/` and probes under `explorations/perf-probes/transactions/`.

Gates that must stay green: `AtomicFieldCompiled`, `VarFieldCapturedCompiled`, `AtomicExprCompiled`, `ExitOutOfAtomicCompiled`, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`). No change to walk.
- Before: row 641's numbers, the array loop at 23.17 ns against 8.39 ns an element with the check removed, and no number for a var field. Time a var-field loop with `explorations/perf-probes/transactions/run.sh`, at one and at four threads.

## 12. A walk refusal test that passes on the base

**What the pass means.** The test does not test my fix. By F-383, walk's harness counts a static error that a phase raises before the run, such as the disambiguator's, as a refusal at load. So on the base the program was refused or stopped before running, with some message containing "q". `load_exception_contains=q` is a one-letter key that matches nearly any message naming `q` ("q is undefined", for example) or any word containing the letter. A refusal test must fail on the base (`tests-writing.md`, "The order", step 2). If it passes, find out why before the fix.

**What I do about the walk test.**
1. Run the program on the base under walk and read the message it gave. That is the base's refusal or static error.
2. Correct the program so that, apart from the new overload shape, it is valid and runs clean on the base: fix whatever earlier error it had.
3. Set the key to the full message, `load_exception_contains=illegal overload of q`.
4. With "Expected failure:" echoed, run it through `harness-one.sh` on the base. It must be red because walk loads and runs it. Then apply the fix and see it green.

If the base's error turns out to be a real refusal of the same program for another reason, that is a finding to record, and the test needs a program that only the new check refuses.

**Recording the compiled failure.** F-103 says that one `XXX` file cannot express "compiles, then fails at run time". A single `XXX` compile test with `compile_err_contains` is red, "Saw wrong failure", when the program compiles. So I use the run-time pair (`tests-writing.md`, "Writing an `XXX` test"):
